canonical_statement: The trial evaluated efficacy and safety of empagliflozin 10 mg and 25 mg versus placebo as add-on therapy in people with T2DM uncontrolled on metformin plus sitagliptin.
The trial randomized 172 participants with type 2 diabetes across 26 sites in South Korea.

population.label: Adults in South Korea with type 2 diabetes inadequately controlled on stable metformin plus sitagliptin

canonical_statement: Eligible participants were 19 to 85 years old with type 2 diabetes, screening HbA1c 7.0%-10.0%, BMI 18.5-40.0 kg/m2, and at least 8 weeks of stable oral antihyperglycemic therapy.

population.label: Eligibility criteria
inclusion_criteria: Stable oral antihyperglycemic therapy for at least 8 weeks

canonical_statement: Participants entering the treatment period after the run-in were required to have HbA1c 7.0%-10.0%.
Key renal exclusions included eGFR below 45 mL/min/1.73 m2, end-stage renal disease, or ongoing dialysis.
Key metabolic exclusions included type 1 or secondary diabetes, prior acute/chronic metabolic acidosis including diabetic ketoacidosis, and screening FPG above 270 mg/dL.

population.label: Metabolic exclusion criteria
exclusion_criteria: History of acute or chronic metabolic acidosis including diabetic ketoacidosis

canonical_statement: Recent acute cardiovascular events or unstable heart failure within 24 weeks before screening were exclusion criteria.

population.label: Recent cardiovascular exclusion criteria
exclusion_criteria: Acute myocardial infarction, cardiovascular shock, ischemic stroke, cerebral hemorrhage, transient ischemic attack, acute or unstable heart failure, or unstable angina within 24 weeks

canonical_statement: Pregnancy or lactation and inability or unwillingness to use adequate contraception were exclusion criteria.
Participants randomized to empagliflozin 10 mg added the drug to maintained metformin and sitagliptin background therapy.
Participants randomized to empagliflozin 25 mg added the drug to maintained metformin and sitagliptin background therapy.
The control group received placebo add-on for 24 weeks while metformin and sitagliptin were maintained.
After week 24, the placebo group switched to empagliflozin 10 mg for the 28-week extension, while the continuous empagliflozin groups maintained assigned doses.
The trial used a randomized, double-blind, multicentre, therapeutic confirmatory phase 3 design with a 24-week treatment period and 28-week extension.
Randomization used an interactive web response system in a 1:1:1 ratio and was stratified by baseline HbA1c (<=8.5% vs >8.5%) and eGFR (45-<60, 60-<90, >=90 mL/min/1.73 m2).

Patients, investigators, and sponsor remained blinded during the first 24 weeks; after the week-24 database lock, only sponsor members involved in analysis and regulatory reporting were unblinded while investigators, patients, and other sponsor members remained blinded during extension.
Rescue therapy was considered for FPG >240 mg/dL at least twice or investigator determination, using lifestyle intervention or glimepiride up to 4 mg/day.
The primary efficacy endpoint was change in HbA1c from baseline to week 24.
Key secondary endpoints included changes in HbA1c and FPG through week 52 and proportions achieving HbA1c <7% or <6.5% at weeks 24 and 52.
Exploratory endpoints included body weight, waist circumference, UACR, and metabolic syndrome resolution at weeks 24 and 52.

concept.text: Exploratory metabolic and renal surrogate endpoints

canonical_statement: Safety assessment included TEAEs, ADRs, SAEs, serious ADRs, vital signs, laboratory tests, and physical examination.

The primary endpoint used ANCOVA with randomization stratification factors as covariates and a prespecified gatekeeping sequence of empagliflozin 10 mg versus placebo followed by 25 mg versus placebo.
Secondary and exploratory endpoints were analyzed without multiplicity adjustment.

The full analysis set required at least one dose and at least one post-dose HbA1c measurement; safety included all exposed patients; a per-protocol set excluded major protocol deviations, rescue therapy, and adherence below 80%.
Missing efficacy and exploratory values in the full analysis set were imputed using last observation carried forward; safety analyses used observed data without imputation.
The study assumed a -0.7 percentage-point HbA1c treatment difference, SD 0.93%, 90% power, two-sided alpha 5%, and 15% dropout, yielding a planned sample of 165 (55 per group).
Of 230 screened patients, 172 were randomized; 162 completed the 24-week treatment period, 158 entered the extension, and 151 completed the study.
The treatment-period full analysis set included 171 participants: empagliflozin 10 mg n=57, empagliflozin 25 mg n=58, and placebo n=56.
The full analysis set had mean age 60.4 years (SD 11.1) and 63.7% men.
Baseline mean HbA1c was 7.8% (SD 0.6) and mean FPG was 152.1 mg/dL (SD 34.7).
Baseline mean BMI was 25.5 kg/m2 (SD 3.1), mean waist circumference 89.8 cm (SD 8.3), and mean eGFR 89.3 mL/min/1.73 m2 (SD 13.6).
At baseline, 56.1% of participants had hypertension and 86.0% had dyslipidemia.
At week 24, empagliflozin 10 mg reduced HbA1c versus placebo by an adjusted mean difference of -0.7 percentage points (95% CI -1.0 to -0.4; p<0.0001).
At week 24, empagliflozin 25 mg reduced HbA1c versus placebo by an adjusted mean difference of -0.8 percentage points (95% CI -1.1 to -0.5; p<0.0001).
At week 24, empagliflozin 10 mg reduced FPG versus placebo by an adjusted mean difference of -32.2 mg/dL (95% CI -41.4 to -23.1; p<0.0001).
At week 24, empagliflozin 25 mg reduced FPG versus placebo by an adjusted mean difference of -32.6 mg/dL (95% CI -42.0 to -23.1; p<0.0001).
At week 52, the mean HbA1c change from baseline in the continuous empagliflozin 10 mg group was -0.7% (SD 0.7).
At week 52, the mean HbA1c change from baseline in the continuous empagliflozin 25 mg group was -0.7% (SD 0.8).
At week 52, the placebo-to-empagliflozin 10 mg switch group had a mean HbA1c change from baseline of -0.6% (SD 0.8).

The authors concluded that empagliflozin add-on to sitagliptin and metformin safely improved glycemic control in Korean patients with T2DM and described triple therapy as a preferable treatment option with multifaceted effects.
The authors attributed additional benefits to renal protection, weight control, and improvement in metabolic syndrome.
The authors explicitly noted that the study was confined to the Korean population.
The study was funded by Chong Kun Dang Pharmaceutical Company, Seoul, Korea.
Chong Kun Dang Pharmaceutical Company supported investigational-drug supply, clinical monitoring, data management, statistical analysis, and medical writing.
Several authors disclosed consulting, lecture, grant, or external-director relationships with pharmaceutical companies, including Chong Kun Dang for SHL and IKJ.
The datasets generated and/or analyzed during the study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.
Figure 2 has an internal panel-label inconsistency: its caption assigns HbA1c to panel A and FPG to panel B, while the plotted axes/panel letters show panel A as FPG and panel B as HbA1c.

Results prose states that both empagliflozin groups had significantly greater week-24 waist-circumference reductions than placebo, while Table 2 marks a significant placebo comparison only for the 10 mg waist-circumference row.

Results prose states that week-24 systolic blood-pressure reductions in both empagliflozin groups were significantly greater than placebo, whereas Supplementary Table 4 footnotes display only within-group significance markers and no explicit between-group comparison marker.
